speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF DESTRUCTION BY FIRE OF HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Order. As today, February 3, is the anniversary of the tragic destruction of the original House of Commons by fire in 1916, which was accompanied by some loss of life, I have taken the liberty of reminding the house of that event by asking the Sergeant-at-Arms to bring into the house the mace which was used immediately after the fire when the house reassembled several days later.
This is the old, wooden mace made here by the workmen of parliament which was used until the beautiful new gold and silver mace which we now use daily was presented later, in 1916. The new mace and its presentation are described in Beauchesne at page 331. It is familiar to all hon. members. However, I thought perhaps all hon. members did not know that we had two maces, the second being the one which is on the table today and which served the house as the symbol of its authority during the interval between the fire in February and the presentation of the new mace in June of 1916.
If I have erred, the regular mace can be fetched, but I thought hon. members would permit the liberty which I have taken.

Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to stabilize the price of hogs to producers for the calendar year 1961 by a deficiency payment program similar to that in effect during 1960. The support price to producers has been established at $22.65 per hundredweight, national basis, which is approximately 83.5 per cent of the base or ten-year average price of $27.11 per hundredweight.
Under the deficiency payment method of support the board will determine at the end of the year the national average price to producers at which grade A hogs were sold, 90205-6-108J
and if this average price is less than the national support price of $22.65 per hundredweight then a deficiency payment equal to the difference will be made to each registered producer on a maximum of 100 grade A or B hogs.
The action taken by the government last year in placing hog support on a deficiency payment basis has had the anticipated effect of eliminating the previous surplus production and greatly improving hog prices. Over the past year prices to producers have averaged approximately $1 per hundredweight more than the national support price. A year ago the price for grade A hogs at Toronto was $23.65. It is now $29, and has been at or above that level for some time.
There is a very real danger that present prices may encourage a level of hog production which could lead to heavy supplies and much lower prices later this year. While some expansion in production can be accommodated, a warning must be sounded to producers against overexpansion at this time. This situation is widely recognized, and provincial departments of agriculture and others are calling attention to it.
Under these circumstances it is important that the government should not take any steps which could be interpreted as an encouragement to greater production. It has, therefore, been decided to retain the national support price for 1961 at the same level as that of the past year.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement by the minister is a repetition of the policy followed by the government last year in employing the principle of deficiency payments with regard to hogs rather than continuing them under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. What was said last year in this connection, of course, bears repetition now; that is, that the use of the deficiency payment principle will mean that the farmers will not know in advance the price which they will receive as they do with regard to products under the Agricultural Stabilization Act.

CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That the first report of the standing committee on banking and commerce presented to the house on Wednesday, February 1, 1961, be now concurred in.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an objection to this motion that I should like to state. I shall try to state it briefly and remain relevant to the point at all times. I am quite concerned with the practice that is growing up of committee chairmen, when they present reports to the House of Commons, asking for leave to move concurrence the same day. The significance of that practice is that the report must then be read by the Clerk to the house. Depending on the length of the report, considerable time is taken up that otherwise would not be taken up if leave to proceed with the motion the same day was not asked.
Ordinarily the report is merely presented at the table and it then appears in Votes and Proceedings where all hon. members can read it. When concurrence is moved at a later stage the members have before them the report and know what is being dealt with. I venture the opinion that the vast majority of members have not the opportunity of hearing a report when concurrence is moved on the same day the report is presented.
Apparently the practice of asking for unanimous consent to move concurrence on the same day has now become standard. This is

a small point. I mention it because it is a procedure that takes considerable time of the house, and that time is lost from what would be more urgent business. I think it should be mentioned, and I should like particularly to draw it to the attention of the house leader for his consideration. There may be, of course, and undoubtedly there are, cases where it is necessary to ask for unanimous consent. There can be no objection if there is some reason for it; there is objection when there is no reason for asking for such unanimous consent.
My second point is that the motion now before the house asks for concurrence in a report of the standing committee on banking and commerce. The committee report contains three paragraphs; first, that the quorum be reduced from 20 to 15 members; second, that the committee be empowered to print its evidence and proceedings. As far as I am concerned there can be no objection to these two paragraphs.
The third paragraph asks that the committee be given leave to sit while the house is sitting. Now, in certain years this is the committee to which the decennial revision of the Bank Act is referred, and special circumstances may arise in those years; in other years there may be special items of business before the House of Commons which would be referred to this committee and which would require special consideration.
We had a particularly bad experience in this committee some three sessions ago when the estate tax legislation was referred to it. On that occasion the committee sat while the trade and commerce estimates were first being considered in the house, and it will be remembered that trade was quite an important matter at that time. Last year we also had considerable argument in the committee, which I do not wish to go into now, when the combines legislation was being considered. Many hon. members felt that they were being improperly denied their right to attend to their duties in the chamber because very important combines legislation was before the committee and the committee was needlessly sitting at the very hour the particular matters in which they were interested were being considered in the House of Commons. Again that is a matter about which there will be differences of opinion.
The committee can only be a body having delegated authority from the House of Commons, and when the committee has no occasion to seek this special power from the house I can see no reason why it should do so as a matter of course. It is rather interesting that the mover of the motion did not even find it necessary to state to hon. members what particular legislation he expected

to come before the committee which would require members to absent themselves from the House of Commons in order to attend committee sittings.
I would hope that we could revert to the practice of only asking for this power in cases where a committee is able to foresee the necessity of using such power. That situation undoubtedly arises in the committee on agriculture, in that it is necessary to bring officials of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners before the committee. When that situation arises I think it meets with the wishes of all hon. members that these gentlemen, because of the nature and importance of their duties, should be heard in continuing sessions of the committee, and of necessity that involves the committee sitting while the house is also sitting.
A similar situation arises in the case of the special committee on railways which deals with the annual reports of Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. Obviously there is a special need for that committee to ask for this extraordinary delegation of power from the house, but I see no reason for it in the case of the banking and commerce committee at this session of parliament.
I desired to place my objections on record so that hon. members might be fully aware of what is taking place.
As I understand the procedure, it is not possible for the house to amend a committee report. We cannot do that. I have no desire whatever to hold up the commencement of the work of the committee or to object to the other two parts of the committee report, but I propose to submit for the consideration of the house an amendment to the motion which I think is in order. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
That the motion be amended by inserting the words "paragraphs 1 and 2 of" after the word "that" and before the word "the".
The motion would then read:
That paragraphs 1 and 2 of the first report of the standing committee on banking and commerce be now concurred in.
I think that meets the practice of the house in that it is not open to the house to amend the committee report as such. Hon. members will see that if the amendment is carried the report will be concurred in with respect to the reduction of the quorum and the right of the committee to print its proceedings. The only thing that would be changed in any way is that the committee would not have leave to sit while the house is sitting but would have the right to bring that matter forward again at any time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My impression is that the amendment proposed is in order, but in case
Banking and Commerce Committee any member may think otherwise I should like to refer to Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 323, paragraph 2, before placing the amendment before the house. That citation reads as follows:
A report from a committee cannot be amended by the house, but it must be referred back to the committee.
That is the general principle, namely that it is not competent for the house to change a report or amend it. If it wishes to have a report altered, it must send it back to the committee with the request. Also in citation 320 the practice is reported in these words:
A report may be adopted only in part or an amendment imposing a condition to the motion for concurrence may be moved.
This amendment purports to adopt the report in part without altering the report, leaving the third paragraph in suspense.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, whether or not the motion is in order is a matter that I leave to Your Honour to decide. The point at issue is whether a certain committee of the house shall have the privilege of sitting while the house is in session. This is not a new matter. It has been raised in the house on several occasions in the past. We debated it at some length last year following suggestions by the hon. member for Ottawa West, who gave the example then that he gave this morning with regard to some difficulty in 1959 over attendance in the house affecting the attendance in committees.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is the page number, please?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Page 1434 of Hansard of February 25, 1960. Several times during last session the question of committees sitting while the house was in session was raised, as it had been raised in 1959 and in 1958, and we considered the matter rather carefully. On that occasion I pointed out that the practice is not new. It has been in existence in the House of Commons for many years. 1 gave exact references to the session of 1956 when hon. members opposite were on the treasury benches, and compared that record with ours in 1959. I pointed out that in 1956 152 days were devoted to the business of the session, and that on 52 of those days committees were meeting while the house was in session. I pointed out that in 1959, when we formed the government, there were 127 sitting days of the session and that on 55 of those days committees of the house met while the house was in session. I gave those examples covering two regimes in order to indicate that there was nothing new in the

Banking and Commerce Committee practice of asking the permission of the house for committees to sit while the house was in session.
All of us who have served on committees -and everybody here has had that experience now-deplore the necessity of attending committee meetings when the house is in session, when they would perhaps prefer to be in the house in order to listen to or participate in the debates that are taking place. The pressure of business over the years has indicated that it is essential to give this power to the committees, which can be exercised with discretion. It is up to the committees themselves to determine on what occasions they will hold their meetings while the house is in session.
The hon. member for Ottawa West quite fairly pointed out that there were instances- and he gave instances such as the wheat board, the board of grain commissioners, railway officials of the C.N.R. and officials of T.C.A.-when officials were called to appear before committees, and in order not to keep busy people in the city for several days it has been found appropriate to hold committee meetings morning, afternoon and evening, if necessary, in order to complete the examination of witnesses. That happens with other committees as well. The house in its wisdom over the years has decided that the practice of holding committee meetings while the house is in session is one that cannot be easily avoided.
The hon. member for Ottawa West implies that if a committee wishes this additional privilege, it should come back to the house later in the session and ask for it. However, that procedure would involve more delay- and unnecessary delay-because I am sure that if any committee not having the power to sit while the house is in session came back to the house and asked for that power, we should be obliged in reason to accede to that request. We might just as well do it at the start of the session when the committees are being set up. It is open to any member of the opposition who is a member of a committee to raise his objection in that committee if a meeting of the committee is called at what in his opinion seems to be an inappro-propriate time. That has been the practice over the years. I see no reason for changing it.
The arguments advanced this morning by the hon. member for Ottawa West are not dissimilar to those advanced in the past. Yet in view of the figures I have given I think it is obvious that in ordinary sessions such as those in 1956 and 1959-and by "ordinary" I mean in the sense of commencing early in the year and carrying on to midsummer- the actual number of days when committees

meet while the house is in session is about one third of the total. I am not sure of the figures for last year.
However, with the discussion that we had a year ago, I think the committee chairmen and the committee members are fully aware of the situation, and there is no question about the experience of the house now with regard to committee work. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we would not be able to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member.

speechtext:
As the minister has pointed out, Mr. Speaker, this is not the first occasion on which this disagreement has arisen in this house. I do not know whether we are gaining ground or losing ground. I notice that, as the minister stated, the matter was raised on February 25 last year. Here we are again, off to a blanket start, and it is now being raised on February 3. I therefore do not really know whether we have gained a month or lost a month. However, apparently we find ourselves in the same situation as that in which we found ourselves not only last session but in previous sessions as well.
The minister pointed out that the matter is not a new one, and he went back to previous administrations to prove his point. I should like to point out to the minister that, while it may be nothing new, certainly in the opinion of this party, if something is bad that was carried on by a previous administration, there is no reason why it should be carried on under the present one.
I think the dispute is a simple one. It is a question of whether permission should be granted to these committees to sit while the house is sitting, when it becomes necessary to do so, or whether blanket approval should be given at the start of the session. We are certainly consistent in our view on this matter. We opposed this procedure previously. We do not think it is right or proper that it should be done at this time. We do not think it is fair to the members. We are certainly pleased to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I might say that we are glad to note that, contrary to the situation two sessions ago, the Liberals are now in full agreement with this group.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is just one point I should like to add, and it is this. The amendment deals with one committee and one committee alone. The remarks of the house leader dealt with the over-all position and the practice that had grown up in the past in all committees. The point that we on this side of the house are making and have made is that for this particular committee there is certainly no necessity at

this time of the session to sit while the house is sitting. That consideration was pointed out to the chairman and the members of that committee when this organization meeting took place, for some of the reasons that were given by the hon. member for Ottawa West. However, those reasons did not commend themselves to the committee.
The only point at issue at the moment is the question of necessity. I think there is no necessity at this time of the session for this committee to take these extraordinary powers. There are exceptions in certain of the committees that have been mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa West and the house leader, such as for example the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, because there the officials come and must give their evidence over a period of days. But certainly that consideration does not apply to this committee at all. If it did; if there were an extraordinary case which I have not seen during most of the years I have been here, surely the committee could seek the power of the house at the time. For that reason it seems to me that the amendment is one which should commend itself to the house.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is one point in connection with this matter that I think perhaps requires some airing and it relates, if we are dealing with past attendance in committees and attendance in the house, to the most active members in both places. For instance, in 1959 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who we all know is extraordinarily active in the house, also had by far the highest record with regard to attendance and activities in committees in 1959 as compared with all the rest of the Liberals put together. But I think other hon. members are affected, such as the hon. member for Carleton, who is most active. His record in committees and in the house shows that he is one of the most active members. The hon. member for Calgary South is another whose attendance in committees and in the house shows that he was one of the most active. I refrain from mentioning statistical information relating to those of us in the C.C.F., perhaps for reasons of modesty.
In any event, I think this indicates that having committees sit while the house is sitting denies to the most active members of the house the right to participate fully in our affairs. I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Calgary South are cases in point. Perhaps this procedure merely does nothing but cater to a degree to the laziness of some of us who want to get out of the full performance of
Banking and Commerce Committee our duties in the house. I could perhaps understand the desire of this particular committee to sit while the house is sitting if it was doing something or if it was engaged in some important activity in this particular session, or if there was any indication given as to what its activities might be. In this regard I might say that perhaps one of such matters might be the drug industry and the pharmaceutical houses.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That matter is not at issue.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: This is an important matter. This consideration would perhaps be some justification for this committee functioning as desired by their report. Apart from that, however, I think we have no other course but to be consistent and protect members like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Carleton, just to mention two, and also the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who is another who is most active in committees and in the house. It is to protect their activities and in order to give them every opportunity to participate fully this session, as they did in other sessions, and not really to cater to the laziness on the part of some members and their inclination to shirk their responsibilities.

I know many of us in this committee are, as the hon. member for Ottawa West mentioned, somewhat freshmen. I am not the chairman of the committee; I am only presenting this on behalf of the chairman. I do not think there has been any great injustice in the carrying out of the proceedings of these committees.

Banking and Commerce Committee
Last year we were very careful to try to avoid unnecessarily sitting while the house was in session. Perhaps many of the difficulties that arose last year were not so much because this particular committee was sitting during the time the house was sitting, but because of the number of committees. Perhaps there should have been greater co-ordination between the various committees when sitting.
I suggest that there are occasions when we bring witnesses from out of town, and we might find in the morning that we are not able to complete their testimony. It is then too late to ask permission to sit during the rest of that day and we find ourselves having to hold those witnesses over. It seems to me only good business to accept this provision, in view of that difficulty which is foreseen. This would prevent us being put in an embarrassing position.
I would urge that the house accept the motion as presented. Although I am not the chairman of the committee I can undertake, as a member of the committee, to see that we do not abuse the privilege that is given to us.

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. Is he in a position to say what is Canada's attitude regarding the reported suggestion that when Prime Minister Macmillan visits the United States early in April he will take with him a detailed commonwealth disarmament plan? Is the Prime Minister in a position to state whether this is a fact and, if it is, what is the view of the Canadian government in connection with this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON REPORTED COMMONWEALTH PLAN
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has sent me the clippings to which he referred. I think that article reveals a lack of appreciation of the nature of a commonwealth prime ministers' conference. The conference meets for the purpose of the exchange of ideas, not for the determination of policy. Indeed, each of the nations of the commonwealth determines its policies for itself. I would fear greatly if at any time the prime ministers' conference were to arrive at the conclusion that an announcement of a united policy should be made. The danger of so doing would be to create internationally a concept of the commonwealth as an operative bloc.
Having said that, may I add that so far as disarmament is concerned all the nations of the commonwealth are united in their desire to achieve disarmament to the end that the load of expenditures which today rests on all nations may be relieved and international tension may be diminished.
Inquiries of the Ministry
In so far as the conference is concerned, there have been exchanges of views on disarmament, and the Canadian government would like to see included in these exchanges and consultations consideration of the role of the middle and smaller powers in disarmament. speechtext:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Customs Tariff and to provide:
1.	That the said act be amended by adding thereto immediately after section 2 thereof the following section:
"2A. (1) For the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a "class or kind" made or produced in Canada if
(a)	in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada; and
(b)	in the case of goods custom-made to specifications adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
(2)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom-made to specifications shall be deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least ten per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
(3)	The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time."
2.	That subsections (9) and (10) of section 6 of the said act be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(9) For the purposes of this act, notwithstanding section 2A, goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods made or produced in Canada are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade."
3.	That subsection (4) of section 6A of the said act be repealed.
4.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the 21st day of December, 1960, and to have applied to all goods mentioned therein imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was. made before that day.

Mr. Chairman, a well-known volume on Canadian commercial relations has stated that although most tariffs are highly complex the Canadian tariff has been described by the chairman of the tariff board as "easily one of the most complicated in the world." Indeed, a really comprehensive knowledge of all the facets of the Canadain tariff is the work of a lifetime.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Would hon. members please lower their voices when leaving the chamber. It is very difficult to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Because of the complexity of this matter my remarks will be very brief. We have been told that this amendment will mean no higher tariffs but is simply a matter of reclassification where-to use the words of the minister -erosion has taken place in the classification of goods of a class or kind made in Canada. We have been told it will affect some 70 items involving free entry or reduced rates of duty or drawback in respect of specified types of goods when of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada.
I believe that some of the confusion which has resulted has arisen from words that have been placed on Hansard during the debate. We have been told that this is not a high tariff policy, but the hon. member for Stormont in his speech as reported at page 1685 of Hansard commended the minister for introducing-
-this present constructive measure now being brought in to assist and protect the hard beset manufacturers in this country-
If this is not a high tariff measure, and if there is no intention on the part of the government to undertake high tariff policies or a trend toward such policies, how can this measure-and I quote the hon. member's words once again-
-assist and protect the hard beset manufacturers in this country-
The hon. member in the course of his remarks went on to say that there will be no changes in GATT arrangements or in trade agreements with other countries. I suggest that the proposed amendment, though not one which may immediately bring about higher tariff policies, is none the less an open door toward future higher tariffs. As we have seen, there are two methods of determining tariff classification relating to whether goods are of a class or kind made in Canada. The first is to determine whether dumping duties are applicable; the other is to determine the tariff classification for goods which are of a class or kind made in Canada. Surely this proposed legislation will change the entire emphasis and open the door to future higher tariff
Customs Tariff
policies. Will it not mean that the same rules and much wider rules, will apply for purposes of the tariff classification as well as the dumping provision?
I think this is a most interesting innovation. If the government has no intention of raising tariffs, then this should be stated very definitely and some negation of the remarks made by several hon. members in this committee should be made. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with regard to custom-made specifications, no Canadian production is necessary. The only question is whether "adequate facilities exist" for the economic production of goods "within a reasonable length of time." However, the question arises, what are "adequate facilities"; and what is "a reasonable length of time". Indeed, what is "economic production"? Does it contemplate a level of costs above that which would be competitive with the cost of imported goods? Certainly it must. But how high?
In his speech, especially in his remarks in reply to the hon. member for Laurier, the Minister of Finance indicated a belief that Canadian labour was in the vanguard for higher tariffs; that it was beating the drum or sounding the trumpet for higher tariffs. This is an entirely erroneous concept, and I should like to place on Hansard a statement from the very brief which was placed in the hands of the government yesterday morning with respect to tariffs. I shall read a very short quotation which will indicate the position of organized labour and indeed unorganized labour on this matter of tariffs;
Where the industry is dying, or seriously ill, because of import competition, the situation is different. The obvious, simple, easy (deceptively easy) solution to the problem is to slap on a quota or a tariff stiff enough to stop the imports or reduce them to negligible proportions. There are times when this may be the only thing to do, at least temporarily.
Here is the long term policy:
But as a general, permanent policy for dealing with unemployment arising from import competition, this simple, easy policy has several serious defects.
The next two or three pages of the brief are concerned with the defects of the higher tariff policy. This statement has particular relation to the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier-I do not know why I should be defending the hon. member-in regard to the textile workers, who are looked upon as probably the foremost exponents of tariff increases. Statements made in this house in that regard are completely erroneous. I am quoting from the latest official publication of

Customs Tariff
the textile workers. It is an open letter to the Globe and Mail in answer to an editorial, and it reads in part:
For these and other fundamental reasons we have rejected the traditional laissez-faire demand for wage reductions and tariff Increases in favour of increased international trade on a planned basis.
In my remarks I do want to indicate that the Minister of Finance has no fear from labour in this country if the policy of this government is one of lowering tariffs. Labour does not want a "beggar thy neighbour" policy. Labour does not want to export unemployment to some other country or to some other part of this country. We realize that secondary industry produces more of our gross national product than any other sector of the economy; that it provides more employment. But I think secondary industry is coming to realize that higher tariffs, which this amendment appears to be advocating, if the remarks of the hon. member for Stormont are to be given any credence, are a very fallacious argument for increasing prosperity in this nation.
Possibly there were times in the past when a higher tariff policy had some force, and possibly that was true of the national policy of the nineteenth century when Canada found herself beside the large, expanding and very aggressive industrial economy of the United States, so in a sense low tariffs were a serious disadvantage to an infant industry economy. But an infant industry economy argument no longer holds very much water in this country. The position of this group is that the trend or the emphasis which in the long run will direct our Canadian economy toward the establishment of a world market -eventually, not immediately-is the only thing which can be regarded as legitimate in this twentieth century.
The Minister of Finance has indicated that he is concerned with the dumping which is being carried on by other nations. Indeed, this is a serious problem; but I think we should never forget that what we call dumping may be regarded as a legitimate trade practice of the nation which happens to be on the other side of the fence. There is no reason why our use of an emotionally charged word like "dumping" should be an excuse for putting up tariffs which will create inefficient industry by raising the price of machinery or by permitting higher prices, because I think the Canadian public realizes that the consuming public pays for tariffs in a straightforward way just as it pays income taxes every April. There is virtually no difference, except that you can tell a little easier in the former case just where the money is going and where it is coming from.

In looking at this amendment I think we could very well recognize other methods by which we can create more stability and more prosperity in our secondary industry. One way would be by capital assistance on an enlightened taxation system to take the place of this emphasis on higher tariffs. Possibly the setting up of export and import boards would be a great help, and under some kind of a plan we could determine what particular industries do have a place in our Canadian economy, where the raw products and skilled workers are available, and so on. This, I think, would receive the support of the Canadian people.
As I have stated and must repeat in conclusion, the trend must be toward a world economy, a lowering of tariffs and other barriers and an increase in the prosperity of other parts of the world. The emphasis and trend which appear in this particular amendment must be reversed if Canada is to play its part both politically and economically in the world of the twentieth century.

Mr. Chairman, after listening to the hon. member for Peterborough, especially in the last few minutes, it seems to me there was no necessity for him appearing as a New party candidate. He has been talking Liberalism and nothing but Liberalism, and I commend him for doing so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman adopts his words completely, then?

The hon. gentleman makes his own speeches except when he finds it useful to refer to the previous utterances of the Minister of Finance, which sometimes express his thoughts better than his own, and this is going to be one of those occasions. Last night the Minister of Finance attempted to sum up what was said at some greater length by his colleague the Minister of National Revenue about this question of appeals. His words will be found at page 1697 of Hansard, in the first full paragraph, and I read as follows:
On this matter of the right of appeal; this subject, with great respect, has been quite misapprehended. The suggestion is that there has been some narrowing of the effective right of appeal. I submit there is no effective narrowing of the right of appeal contemplated by this legislation.
There is no misapprehension about this matter, and the mere fact that the Minister of Finance says there is does not make it so. As I pointed out last night, it is perfectly clear, to deal only with shelf goods first, that up to now there has been the right of appeal on all questions of fact. Now parliament is being asked to deny the right of appeal on what is quite obviously the most important

of the questions of fact. In other words the taxpayer, or any other party who considered himself aggrieved, formerly could go to the tariff board and have an adjudication, if he appealed on any of those points. He is now to be denied the right of appeal with respect to the normal Canadian consumption.
We were given a very specious argument by the Minister of National Revenue last night that this was a purely statistical matter. If that were true, sir, it seems to me that, if it is a mere matter of fact it should not be excluded from determination by any appeal. The tariff board should not be prevented from looking at this fact and from looking at the source of what is an alleged fact. The tariff board is an independent tribunal, or i s supposed to be, and I think it always has been. Its judgments on points of law are appealable to the courts and public argument can be made before the tariff board, so that the public is let in.
What we are being asked to do in this resolution is to approve the introduction of a bill which will take away from the tariff board altogether that right of appeal on the most important single matter of fact. By doing so this will make a complete farce of any appeal, because the Minister of National Revenue is now going to be able to say finally, without having to produce any facts in support thereof-it is just his word that will determine this-what the normal Canadian consumption is; he can put that at any figure he likes, and that is it. That is what parliament is being asked to say, that the minister may state that in his opinion the normal consumption is such and such and that is it, and all you can then ask the tariff board to decide is whether 10 per cent of that quantity is produced in Canada.
The 10 per cent part is a mathematical operation but the first part, the vital part on which all the rest depends, is to be taken away from appeal. Why? I can follow both ministers when they say they do not like the way in which the courts have, as they say, narrowed the scope of the made in Canada provision. If so, let them come in here honestly and redefine that, but do not take away the right of appeal. I do not even approve of their redefining of it, but that is a separate matter. I am dealing now with this denial of the right of appeal in the most important single element of the whole thing.
Why are they doing this? I ask myself, why are they saying that the tariff board cannot look at this, the most important single element of all, in its adjudication? Why not? One can only suppose that the government has some reason for this, and some reason other than the snide observations made by the Minister of Finance about the tariff board
Customs Tariff
and the courts in which he described their judgments as an erosion. "Erosion" is not a word that lawyers generally apply to judgments of the courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are you speaking as a lawyer now?

The courts are supposed to interpret the law, and as a matter of fact on balance I would rather have the courts interpret the law for me than the Minister of Finance or even the Minister of National Revenue, for whose objectivity I have somewhat more regard than I have for that of the Minister of Finance. But I think this is a position in which no parliament should ever put any minister unless there is absolutely no other course. The Minister of National Revenue has said there is nothing new about this. He has said that he has power now under the Customs Act. He referred to the power to determine valuation for duty purposes under the dumping laws where there is no prescribed method applicable to the case. That is true, and it is quite obvious why it is true. Parliament has laid down a lot of tests, and if none of these tests apply and somebody still wants to import the goods, the minister may decide what the value is. That occurs when there is no criterion at all, but this is a very residual matter and not an unreasonable provision in the circumstances.
But here we are applying this provision to the whole range of commodities that may become subject to the made in Canada provision. In the case of certain goods that are free under the tariff it would not apply of course, and that is also true of certain cases where the duties are absolutely fixed. But having regard to the vast range of our trade, why does the government think the minister should be given the power to decide this thing finally? I grant, of course, that the minister and his officials have to determine all these things in the first instance. That is the only way you can carry on administration, and anybody who has any experience with government knows that.
What we are objecting to more than anything else in this resolution, though we object to almost everything in it, is this eagerness to place arbitrary power in the hands of a single minister. Six years ago the Minister of Finance and other members who now occupy the treasury benches were very eloquent in their objections to certain arbitrary powers which they suggested the government of that day was asking to have conferred for an indefinite period upon the then minister of defence production. Under that legislation those powers could only be exercised at a time of the gravest national peril,

Customs Tariff
and notwithstanding the argument that was put up at that time any lawyer worth his salt knows that if those powers had been exercised at a time other than one of grave national - peril it would have been possible to take a case into the courts and challenge the government in that regard.
But here we are being asked to give a single minister the power to determine at his discretion, without appeal, something which is supposed to be a matter of fact in the normal course of the operation of our trade. There must be some reason for it. It is not just because it would be more convenient. The hon. member for Greenwood has often and eloquently spoken in the house about the question of discretion. He knows, as I know-I am not sure that many other members on the treasury benches remember these things, but he does-that the classic argument for discretion is speed and convenience. I think one can argue that there will be no additional speed or convenience here at all, but that is not the issue. The issue is that this is a power of final determination which it was not thought necessary before to give to the minister. Why are we being asked to do so now?
If I were of a suspicious mind instead of being the naive and innocent person I am, I would suspect that the reason the government is doing this is that an election is approaching and they feel that if there were an unscrupulous minister he could make these determinations in such a way as to give protection in a lot of cases where 10 per cent of the normal consumption is not being produced in Canada at all. All the minister needs to do under this law is to fix the amount of the normal consumption low enough so that whatever little production there may be in Canada is 10 per cent, and then the higher duty applies. It just makes a mockery of any determination, and I would think that any minister who has any regard for our constitutional system, any regard for the courts, any regard for parliament, would not be seeking, without any excuse except that it would be easier or that it is merely statistical, to have this power of life and death over a large part of the business of the country all the time. Surely the practice that wherever it is possible to do so there should be in the subject the power of appealing to a tribunal not under the thumb of the executive is a basic principle of our whole constitution.
Speaking for myself, sir, and I think I can also speak for everybody else over here, I will not be impressed in the slightest degree by any alleged precedents for this action even if they were Liberal precedents. Since they came into office in 1957 hon. gentlemen

opposite, no matter what they do, say "Well, you used to do it". I would remind them and the people of the country that these hon. gentlemen, in making their appeal to the electors said they would change all that and restore the rights of parliament-that is what they said-which they said had been eroded by the Liberals. Now they have produced the very precedents they condemned previously in order to support far more thoroughgoing invasions than anything that was ever proposed in peacetime by the Liberal government.
It is quite true that the powers that were asked for by the government in 1955 under the Defence Production Act were extraordinary powers to which any reasonable person would take objection in normal times, but they were only asked for not in normal times but to meet a critical emergency at a time when the state of the world was, as it still is, very much disturbed.
Whether that case was justified or whether it was not justified, here we are dealing with our normal trade; and the government, through this resolution and the bill to be founded upon it, is seeking to take away a right of appeal which has up to now existed, or to take away an element in that right of appeal which would make the rest of the appeal a complete mockery. The moment the minister decides what the normal consumption is in Canada, everything else flows from it as a mathematical formula.
It would appear to me a great deal simpler and a great deal easier to determine what the production was in Canada. If you were going to give something to the discretion of the minister on the ground that it was statistical, that would be a great deal simpler to determine. After all, most of these commodities are produced in factories the location of which is known, and it would be much simpler. But none of the elements should be excluded from the review if there is to be a review. How can you adjudicate if you are told that you must accept as the truth any statement the minister chooses to make? I hope we are not going to hear anyone on the treasury benches rise in his place and say, "We are such honest and straightforward fellows that we would never do anything wrong."

From another court.

There are many, many cases where there are specific limitations imposed on a right of appeal. Sometimes it is on the jurisdictional aspect; sometimes it is in terms of the amount involved. There are many cases under statutes both of Canada and the provinces where the scope of appeal is limited.
I have pointed out that we do not take away the right of appeal here at all. I want to say, however, that exactly the same fears are felt by the interior lumber manufacturers' association and various separate milling industries in the constituency I have the honour to represent.
I have received a number of telegrams and letters from people in the lumber industry in the interior. I will not take time to go into them to any extent but I will read one which clearly illustrates their attitude:
We feel that amendments proposed in the new section 2(a) of the Customs Tariff Act will increase costs of operation to our industry a primary exporting industry which will result in the lumber industry being placed in less competitive position and add to an already extremely serious economic situation. We agree that encouragement of secondary industry is desirable but it is extremely essential not to place primary industry in a noncompetitive position in our markets.
E. L. Vance, president, Kootenay Forest Products.
I know this gentleman very well. He has long experience in the lumber industry. I can support his claim that the industry is in a serious economic situation at present in the interior of British Columbia owing to the extent of markets and the prices being paid for lumber shipped to those markets. It is presently a marginal operation for the operators in that area. That is why they are concerned about the amendment to the Customs Tariff proposed by this legislation.
If the minister rises to speak again perhaps he would give us the reason why he is amending the Customs Tariff in this respect using what is considered even by laymen who are not familiar with legal matters to be somewhat ambiguous language likely to be open to many interpretations. I have been asked why this has been done and why ambiguous words are used. The words that are particularly objectionable are "approximately the same class or kind made or produced in Canada". The word "approximately" whether viewed in its dictionary meaning or looked at from its application in daily life is a word the meaning of which varies according to personal imagination and one's understanding of the English language.
I should like the minister to tell us why he has made this alteration. I trust he will give consideration to the reasonable fears expressed by the lumber industry in toto in British Columbia and, as far as I am concerned, particularly in the interior where operating conditions are ever more difficult than in the coastal area.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member was not in the committee last night when a similar question was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I believe I dealt with it quite fully in reply. The hon. member will find my observations on this subject at pages 1683 to 1685 of Hansard. The hon. member for Vancouver East raised the question as to the word "approximately" and asked for my comment on the alternative suggestion put forward by the Vancouver board of trade in this respect. I dealt with that and the hon. member will find my observations on that subject beginning at the bottom of the second column of page 1684 where, I think, the reasons are given quite fully.
I should like to make what I hope will be a relatively brief observation upon some of the remarks made this morning by the hon. member for Peterborough. Let me say that in general I liked the hon. member's speech very much. It was to my liking not because I approve what he was contending for but because I thought it was a very useful exposure of the fact that if the hon. member typically represents the new party it will not be the spokesman or even the pretended spokesman of labour in this country very long because the speech that the hon. gentleman made was just about as inimical to the interests of labour in Canada as I suppose any speech that any of us has heard in this chamber for a very long time.
Peterborough is a riding that has unhappily had considerable unemployment. Perhaps the hon. member owes his election to that unhappy circumstance. But I may tell the hon. member that in the course of this past decade the kind of attrition to which I have made reference before has greatly weakened and subtracted from the benefits that these provisions in the Customs Tariff were intended to provide for industries and their employees in places like Peterborough. These benefits have been whittled away. That is one of the reasons why there has been unemployment in places like Peterborough.
When we bring forward here a measure to restore to these words the value that they had up until the decade of erosion this hon. member rises in his place and opposes this legislation and in the course of doing so makes statements which show that if he has any knowledge of labour and labour's problems and any knowledge in relation to the problem of unemployment, his knowledge is not more than academic, in my opinion.
The hon. member talked as though this legislation were the expression of a high tariff policy. It is nothing of the kind. I gave an abundance of evidence last night to indicate that this government has loyally observed
Customs Tariff
all the provisions of GATT and that in the three budgets that have been introduced since we came into office in which there have been tariff changes there have been more tariff items reduced than there have been increased. I pointed out some of the things that a government could have done under the existing legislation if it had been minded to use it in pursuance of a high tariff policy. We had only to change by order in council the present percentage defined in pursuance of the powers conferred by section 6, subsection 10 of the Customs Tariff, but we have not done that and we are proposing to give that power back to parliament.
I say that this committee, the people of Peterborough and people outside the riding of Peterborough will be interested to know whether the hon. gentleman who is a member of the new party can be regarded as a champion of the rights of labour and they have evidence to the contrary on the basis of the speech the hon. member made today. The hon. gentleman had the opportunity to show himself as the champion of the rights of labour, a man interested in the employment possibilities of legislation of the kind now under debate, but he has chosen instead to denounce the legislation and in that way to deprive industries in Peterborough and their employees of the benefit that this legislation was intended to give them and which they did enjoy prior to the erosion of the past ten years.
I can tell the hon. member that the delegations which have appeared before my colleague the Minister of National Revenue and before me in regard to matters related to the terms of competition of Canadian producers and Canadian workmen with imports from abroad do not tell us the things that he has told the committee today. There is a deep gulf fixed between the point of view which he exposed in this house today and the point of view that is put before my colleague and myself by the authentic voice of organized labour in appearing before us.
The minister does not think the electors have an authentic voice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they do, but it has to be remembered that at times the electors send people here on a minority vote and that members arrive here without having the endorsement of the majority of their electors and that sometimes-
I did not suffer that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-they are misled as to the position, the platform, the attitudes and the sympathies of those they elect, and sometimes it takes time for them to find out. They are finding out that-

The minister is right, they are finding out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are certainly finding out and they are going to find out a great deal more on this subject, and what was said here this morning I think will be of considerable assistance not only to the electors of Peterborough but to the electors of other constituencies who may be intending to support candidates of the new party on the theory, the now discarded theory, that they are authentic spokesmen for labour and for the rights of labour.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not now; I wish to finish what 1 am saying.
The minister has heard the voices; would he be specific on those voices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I took several questions from the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate and he made a speech every time. I wish to develop a point. I will take the hon. member's question later.
The hon. member for Peterborough tried this morning to put the Canadian Congress of Labour on the side of low tariffs. While it is true that in the brief put forward yesterday attention was drawn by the congress to the fact that tariff increases, as it is put here, "would not provide any real solution to this problem", that is, the essential problem of the plight of secondary industries in the face of import competition, yet, Mr. Chairman, that is not all that the congress has said, and that is not all that the congress has represented.
Two years ago the congress appeared before the cabinet, and they also made their representations. It happened to come just after a hearing before the tariff board in regard to the imports of rubber footwear coming into the country in heavy volume at that time, both from Hong Kong and Japan. Following that decision of the tariff board, this is what the Canadian Congress of Labour had to say in its memorandum to the government of Canada dated January 22, 1959. I quote:
We are naturally disappointed at the recent tariff board decision not to afford protection to the rubber footwear industry. This may prove to be the death knell of this long established Canadian industry and seriously affect the future of the small towns in which most of the industry is located. The condition of the textile industry continues to be precarious notwithstanding the fact that some increases in tariff have taken place.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, let no hon. member attempt to pretend in this house that the authentic voices of organized labour have not been heard, and heard frequently, by the

government or by individual ministers of the government in receiving their representations on the subject of the terms of the competition faced by Canadian workmen in relation to imports from abroad.
Then, the hon. member made an extraordinary statement in which he said that dumping may be legitimate trade practice. This is a most extraordinary statement. Here we have an hon. member saying that dumping may be a legitimate trade practice. Let me say to him that there is nothing legitimate about dumping.
That is not what the hon. member said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provisions of the GATT-I have not given the floor to the hon. member.
He did not say that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provisions of the GATT make it quite clear that the GATT regards dumping as an inadmissible practice.
He never said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
dumping is the sort of thing that, as a trade practice, has been put under the ban and condemnation of this house over the years, and put there in stronger legislative form in 1958. I hope the hon. member for Peterborough will soon learn that dumping is a practice which is capable of robbing Canadian workmen of their jobs.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member went on to say that we should have import boards, and let the import boards determine what industries have a place in our society. This means that he is proposing that the government should set up boards and take this right away from parliament, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate rose in his place at the end of the speech and said that it was a good Liberal speech. This proposal was to take something out of parliament and put the power in the hands of an import board to say what industries in this country have a place in our economy. Do you realize what that means, Mr. Chairman?
The minister is willing to put it in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is suggested that we confer upon a board, which could be entirely bureaucratic, the right to decide what industries in this country should be marked out for survival and what industries should be marked out for the sentence of economic doom.
The minister prefers to give that power to the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is socialism. It is the kind of socialism that can strangle enterprise; it is the kind of socialism which expresses itself in that kind of bureaucracy. As long as this government is in office it is not going to set up any boards to pronounce the doom of any Canadian industries or pronounce the death knell on the jobs of Canadian workmen. No, Mr. Chairman-
Just a single minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me make it very clear, then, Mr. Chairman, that when we hear what is the first voice in this house of the new party we hear a doctrine that is absolutely inimical to the interests of Canadian workmen, that contemplates the destruction by bureaucratic means of some Canadian industries. If the Canadian people want that, then I do not know the Canadian people. The Canadian people know that with this present administration every reasonable effort is going to be made to give a decent opportunity to Canadian industries and Canadian workmen to compete with the imports that are coming into this country, and to do so at all times with due regard to our obligations under the GATT and to our position as a great exporting nation. We have shown ourselves at all times deeply conscious of the necessity of maintaining those relationships and that position of Canada in the markets of the world.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I leave this subject. This is a doctrine that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in his laudatory remarks, said at the conclusion of the speech this morning by the hon. member for Peterborough-apparently he regarded it as good Liberal doctrine-was a Liberal speech. He hailed it as a Liberal speech, the kind of speech that I say can find a way of pronouncing the doom of Canadian industry and the jobs of Canadian workmen.

The minister knows very well that I did not endorse the whole speech. I endorsed the concluding observation with a degree of praise. I want merely to correct the untrue statement just made by the Minister of Finance. I did not endorse the whole speech of the hon. member at all. I said that his concluding words, which were words of-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
-commendation for the liberation of trade were spoken like a Liberal, or words to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid the record will not bear you out on that.
