The minister indicated that at the proper time he would be prepared to answer my question. In his recent remarks he referred to the voices of labour which he and the government had received.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I understood the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River just wanted to ask a question.
That is right. As you will remember, Mr. Chairman, I rose when the minister was speaking-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Timmins wishes to make some remarks. If the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wishes to ask a question he may do so.

The minister indicated that at the conclusion of his remarks he would be prepared to receive from me the question I had risen to ask him and which he preferred to have at this point. In his remarks with respect to the attitude of the hon. member for Peterborough the minister referred to having received as a minister of the government representations from labour with respect to the tariff question. Would he indicate from what voices of labour in Peterborough he has received approbation of the legislation presented to us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not confine myself to Peterborough; I was not speaking simply about Peterborough. I was speaking about the voice of labour generally. We have had representations from labour organizations and very often the delegations are accompanied by representatives of the labour organizations.

I take it then that the minister suggests that he has heard from labour representatives of the rubber footwear industry but from what other labour representatives whose voice he would respect has he received representations in support of this kind of legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There have been a number of them. I would not attempt to give a complete list now. My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, has also received many of them. We certainly have had representations from labour in the rubber footwear field. We have had representations from labour in the silver flatware field. I have had a number and the Minister of National Revenue has had even more.

Customs Tariff

Mr. Chairman, I should like to correct the misinterpretation that the minister had placed on the comments of the hon. member for Peterborough. The minister has indicated that organized labour wants tariff protection. Organized labour has contended annually for many years now in its presentations to the government of the day that it is not asking for high tariff policies because in the eyes of organized labour high tariff policies rather than providing employment are a major cause of unemployment such as we have in Canada at this time.
This does not mean to say that organized labour is in favour of free trade. Organized labour has continually asked for protection of various enterprises when it is in the national interest to do so. The resolution says that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Customs Tariff so as to provide certain things. I regret that it does not read that it is expedient to introduce a measure to abolish the Customs Tariff and to replace the whole tariff structure with adequate legislation enacted by parliament which would be based on recommendations of export and import boards as to what enterprises in Canada should receive all-out protection, which ones should receive partial protection and which ones should receive no protection whatsoever. To indicate that the hon. member for Peterborough was not adequately defending the interests of labour in Peterborough was a gross misrepresentation indeed because even the people of Peterborough know that high tariffs are not the answer.
The minister has made a great point of advocating that this measure is necessary to provide protection to Canadian industry and supply employment to Canadian labour. It is our contention that the enactment of the legislation which will follow the resolution is going to add to unemployment in Canada in that we will very definitely be handicapped in our efforts to hold down Canadian costs of production. I cannot for the life of me see why machinery entering into either primary or secondary production in Canada could not be exempted from the proposal that the government is now placing before us.
The minister made the statement that this legislation is going to be applauded by the business community of Canada. I have yet to hear any applause anywhere in Canada with respect to the proposed legislation except for the odd real dyed in the wool Tory newspaper editors writing editorial comment on the action proposed by the government. The minister admits that the purpose of the legislation is to raise tariffs and yet when we say that the Tories are raising tariffs there are heated and angry denials as though the loudness, of voice of the minister is going

to make it so. Regardless of the loudness of his voice, a reading of Hansard alone will convince any Canadian that the aim of the government is to use this resolution and the legislation to follow for the sole purpose of raising tariffs on imports into Canada.
The minister claimed that the other member nations of GATT are not complaining. We believe that we have reason to think that other nations have complained in the past about the actions of the Conservative government when at every possible turn they are taking advantage of the loopholes that exist under GATT and, while paying lip service to the principles of GATT, are eroding those principles by the many minor actions that are being undertaken from time to time. That is why I indicated in the budget debate that actions of this kind by member governments are undermining the possible future existence and extension of the very basic principles of GATT.
The minister knows very well that it is not part of our plan to have import boards arrive at decisions as to what enterprises are to receive adequate protection. Import and export boards are meant to act in an advisory capacity to whatever government happens to be in office at the time and as advisers to legislators generally. We say that there is an alternative to a policy either of high tariffs or of low tariffs and that the whole concept of tariffs in this day and age is outmoded as a useful instrument in the hands of government and has to be replaced. Otherwise we will have either low tariff policies which will ruin legitimate Canadian industries and cause unemployment or we will have high tariffs which in turn will cause unemployment as they have always done in the past.
The minister is very worried about the effect throughout Canada of the election in Peterborough. We are very well aware of that, but I felt that for the minister to attempt to misrepresent the position of labour on the question of tariffs was not in keeping with the debate now taking place. If the minister wants to know the position of labour on the whole subject of tariffs he only has to read the briefs that the organized labour movement as a whole has presented to the government over many long years now. While labour contends that a policy of high tariffs is not the answer to unemployment, labour also realizes that there are industries in Canada which in many cases may need not merely partial protection but all-out protection through the actions of the government of the day.

I should like to ask a question of the hon. member who has just

spoken. If I understood him correctly, he suggested that industry should be controlled by boards so that they could set tariffs to protect the industry that needed protection and the industry that did not need protection. I was wondering whether he thought the same boards or boards of a different type should control organized labour at the same time.

Mr. Chairman, I was not even recommending that the import or export board should control anyone. The import or export board should only look at the statistics and the facts and, bearing all factors in mind, make known to legislators their findings. I see no reason why we should not have a policy whereby we import into the lower mainland of British Columbia a fixed amount of potatoes at certain definite seasons of the year without the handicap of a tariff and at other times, when it may be deemed in the national interest, block them from ruining our own Canadian producers.

This is the first opportunity I have had to speak, Mr. Chairman, except to ask a question, since the Minister of National Revenue spoke before the luncheon adjournment and for a few minutes after the luncheon adjournment. We may have had some fairly strong language used in the consideration of this resolution. I think perhaps it is justified because some great changes are being made in connection with historic patterns with reference to goods of a class and kind made in Canada or not made in Canada; and this is so despite what the Minister of Finance has tried to suggest to this committee.
The Minister of Finance makes a statement and he perhaps thinks we are naive enough to accept it as being important. He says this legislation presented to us now involves no change in rates. What could be more fatuous or more out of line in real meaning than a statement of that kind? The minister himself is the author of the statement in this debate that some 70 items of great consequence in our tariff schedules involve rates of tariff duty which ultimately go down into our economy as an expense to our consumers, and they involve rates that could be for the most part either 7J per cent or 22J per cent. That is an increase of 15 per cent.
In the strict interpretation of his words the Minister of Finance may be truthful when he says that what is before us is not making any change in tariff rates in so far as what is before us is not changing the numerals in the tariff schedule with respect to any of these important items. However, I hope no member of the committee will be misled in the slightest degree into thinking that if we 90205-6-1104
Customs Tariff
are changing the rules upon which there is judgment as to what article is made in Canada as against what article is not made in Canada we are not here in this committee in effect making a great change perhaps in the rate of tax that will apply to the articles involved.
In particular, it has been made evident that in respect of articles that are described here as goods custom-made to specifications we are dealing with extremely expensive items; and perhaps, even more important, we are dealing with items that are of the kind that would be purchased by our broad base of producers and manufacturers across this country. I refer to machinery and heavy articles of custom-made goods.
Everyone whom I have heard who is entitled to respect these days in connection with some of our economic difficulties always includes in his speech a reference to the importance of not only doing something in the nature of increased production for our domestic market, he also emphasizes the importance of getting into the export market. I suggest that nothing could be more fatal to that wide group of producers or manufacturers than not to make sure that they are not subject to costs in connection with their original capital costs, particularly related to the machinery of their production, that would first of all perhaps deter them from entering into new fields of endeavour or, in replacement of existing plant, would prove so expensive as to cost of this machinery in relation to what they could get in the cheapest market that it would prove that they could not compete effectively in the export markets of the world.
The hon. member for Vancouver East referred to briefs that he had received from a number of important industries in this country represented in his province of British Columbia. They were notably, I admit, in the extractive and resources industries. On the other hand, however, this consideration goes right through the piece. As far back as 1890, I believe, when a Conservative government was in power, that government despite the pressure that a Conservative government generally gets from manufacturers in this country and quite irrespective of the interests of consumers, through the then minister of finance, namely Mr. Foster, perhaps for the first time decided that this item "of a class or kind made in Canada" was important. He recognized then that one must not look solely to the plant and its labour which would create these machines which involve capital expenditures but that one, in looking to the broad interests of all Canadians, must look to the necessity of making sure that the entire level of manufacturers in this country were given a break to the extent that the costs of

Customs Tariff
capital equipment were not originally priced at such a point beyond international figures that they could not ultimately compete with their international competitors. That idea is of the essence here because we have had an admission that these items described as goods custom-made to specifications are of the essence of the debate that we have been pursuing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: It is the first time it has really been raised.

In this area we also find our chief concern because, despite the comment a moment ago of the Minister of National Revenue, it is in this sphere where we suggest improperly, undesirably and with perhaps havoc to the country, we are giving ministerial final discretion and we are taking away the opportunity of people affected to have the right of appeal to an outside tribunal beyond politics and beyond the minister, a tribunal that has its decisions even subject to appeal through our normal courts, namely the exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada.
It is here where I feel there is no justification whatsoever for this legislation. We will not support the loose phrases that are in this definition. To my mind the word "approximately" practically makes a nonentity of anything serious in connection with this legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman suggest.

I think perhaps I could suggest something more definitive and accurate. That, of course, is not my responsibility. The hon. member for Carleton may hear an amendment that may be more accurate in that respect. I do not know whether or not he is inviting that.
But certainly by dictionary definition, or by reason of the particular power given to the minister to interpret the word "approximately", this language is unduly loose, wide, indefinite and uncertain. I think this is the centre of the ministerial final and ultimate decision that is involved in these matters.
I insist again that this is not going to assist industry in this country to embark on new enterprises. I am convinced that uncertainties will prevail when these matters are not subject to judicial, open and known decisions, when these decisions come from a back room and are final in the office of the Minister of National Revenue, case by case, and because of the looseness of the language that prevails here industry will be discouraged from taking the initiative and deciding

to take a chance on introducing some new endeavour into the industrial activity of this country.
I thought this point was most effectively made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate today. I still think that, while we heard about "Alice in the Looking Glass" and some other off-base comments, no minister has given this committee an adequate answer to that important question which was raised. The question was this: If you are proposing that there should be a redefinition to describe a class or kind of goods that are produced in Canada, why do you not give it to the parliament of Canada to study, and why do you not allow our courts -not a political office-to determine in the future whether a particular item of goods does or does not meet the specifications that the parliament of Canada has in its judgment determined are proper, even if it is by revised and more up-to-date language, having regard to the decisions of certain judicial courts which were referred to in the debate yesterday?
I think this is of the essence. The minister says that over the history of this country there have not been many appeals. Of course that simply emphasizes the necessity for maintaining this right on the part of every Canadian, with respect to a tax, to have a right of appeal beyond the political level, rather than to reduce and deny that right as in substance is being done in this legislation.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. minister a question. Has the minister attempted to figure out what change there might be in budget revenues as a result of these amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is impossible to try to delineate or prophesy the amount of revenue which would be effected by any of these rulings. Obviously such rulings as might be made according to the dire prophecies of my hon. friends opposite will result in a substantial addition to the national revenue.
If there is further protection there will be additional revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
There will be additional
revenue; there is no question of that. How I can answer it otherwise, I do not know. That is the one intelligent comment that my hon. friend has made during the day's debate, and I welcome his return to sanity. However, I do not think there is anything one can say of a specific nature. As a "class or kind" ruling of that nature is made it does, as my hon. friend pointed out, attract a higher rate of duty.
Which is not paid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Of course it is paid.
I realize I was going against my own argument-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is nothing new.

-because my point was that the article might prove to be 15 per cent more expensive by reason of customs duty only, and we all know that every businessman also takes a fee for financing the original cost of his merchandise. So there would be a subsequent mark-up over the 15 per cent before the machinery, perhapss reached the ultimate consumer. There would be discouragement to even starting out by purchasing capital goods of that nature. But in the end perhaps, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, it would mean even less revenue than now; and of course we would have less employment than now, or less employment than possible, because of the fictitious costs provided at the original base of starting up a factory which would provide jobs.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few factual questions that I would like to ask. My first question is this. I assume- and I base it on an assumption, and my assumption may be wrong-that the reason the government now proposes to bring custom-made goods within the ambit of the "made in Canada" provision is that they have had representations made to them that there are cases where, if the duty were high enough, these goods could be made in Canada. I assume that representations have been made to the government and that the government is aware of industries where this could take place. X think before we are asked to make this quite revolutionary change in the law we should be told precisely what those industries are.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, goods of this kind are not being brought in for the first time. There have been rulings on custom-made goods. I have made rulings myself within the last 18 months on goods of the custom-made kind. You get a cartel-

I think I have not made my question clear and I am sure the minister does not want to answer a question the answer to which does not interest me. What is revolutionary about this is that the minister may decide there is a capacity to make them in Canada, instead of the 10 per cent that is made in Canada. I am interested in finding out just what are the categories of industry, manufacture and all other forms of production about which the government has had representations that has led them to think
Customs Tariff
that if this change is made in the Customs Tariff there will be greater production in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Yes. I think the question can be answered "yes".

I should like to know what they are. Normally when a change is made in the Customs Tariff it is not made in vacuo simply because somebody has had an airy fairy notion that it might have some effect. These changes are based on concrete information, either information which the government has assembled itself or more usually because it has been lobbied, because certain people have approached them and said: We could make a certain kind of bulldozer which has never before been made in Canada, but we cannot make it to compete on the basis of the duty on that article at the present time; if the duty were 15 per cent higher, we could do it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Certainly, it would not apply to bulldozers. There, you might get that iniquitous word to which so much objection has been raised, the word "approximately". There might be a question of whether it could lift five tons or five and a half tons, or whether the shovel capacity was three yards or three and a half yards. I am not an industrialist, and I am not speaking with the tone of authority which the hon. gentleman has adopted all day in dealing with these questions. I am not speaking pontifically about all these things. The hon. gentleman has spoken about what goes on in pressure groups and lobbies-subjects with which we are not accustomed, though perhaps we shall be more accustomed to them after 23 years.
What could come in, for example, would be atomic reactors; a thermogenerator could be one of those articles; material and equipment of that kind, which is very heavy equipment of the type which is being increasingly used today because of the change in technology.
The great change in technology which has accompanied the introduction of atomic energy has only developed in the past few years in this country. We first developed our hydroelectric energy. We have harnessed, to a large extent, the streams and rivers at our disposal where this can be done economically. The St. Lawrence waterway is perhaps one of the last we have here in this area of Canada. The Columbia river is another river to which this government is paying attention, and great progress is being made there.
But having exhausted the economic development of hydro you then get thermogenerators. These are, of course, made to specification; they'are custom-made. It takes, I am told, a long while to make them. These

Customs Tariff
are some of the fields in which this legislation may be used in the future to provide employment for Canadians and the development of Canadian industry.

I must say that is pretty vague stuff as, I think, the minister will admit. The hon. gentleman is going to have to decide three questions here. It seems to me that under subsection 3 (b) he will have to make a final decision whether the goods are custom-made to specifications. I admit that is probably not an impossible decision to make.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: An easy one, I think.

It would not always be easy. But the minister has to decide on a much more important question. He must then decide whether adequate facilities exist in Canada. My imagination does not go far enough to enable me to imagine that any government would bring in proposed legislation of this sort unless it had in mind certain specific industries, specific facilities now available in Canada for the manufacture of particular goods which are not now being made in Canada but which the government believes could be made in Canada under the higher duty. It seems to me the government should come clean and tell us what they are. What are we legislating about? Let us have this information in specific terms.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I think I have already
answered that question. I think perhaps the hon. member is being a little more impervious than he usually is, because he apparently wants to stall this debate until five o'clock. I have already said that one example of a machine, or group of machines coupled together, which could be custom-made would be an atomic reactor or a thermogenerator. We have John Inglis who have been working on one; General Electric have been working on one. It is easy enough-I will not say easy; it needs the advice of engineers and inspection by competent officials-but it is a relatively simple matter to determine whether General Electric, for example, can produce a light bulb or whether they can produce a generator or not. These are matters which require an investigation by officials and experts who would then advise in that connection. I am sure the hon. gentleman is not suggesting for one moment that it cannot be determined whether adequate facilities for the production of whatever particular custom-made instrument or engine or productive machinery to which an order may apply exist in Canada or not.

I was not attempting to suggest that. The minister is misunderstanding what I am trying to find out. I am trying to find out where those facilities are at the present time which created in the mind of the government the impulse to bring in this legislation. I do not believe the government dreamed this up. They must have some specific imports in mind which they think could be made in Canada if this legislative change were made. If this is not the case, I think it is irresponsible to ask parliament to deal with the situation.
The government is asking us for a change in our present tariff structure, a change which, because it is clearly protective, is undoubtedly going to arouse hostility among certain of those who at present export goods to Canada. I am not saying this is necessarily a reason why the legislation should not be enacted. I am seeking information. I want to know what facilities exist here which in the view of the government could be used to manufacture goods in place of those now being imported.
I am sure that when Sir John Macdonald introduced the national policy in 1878 he did not just say: if we raise the tariffs a lot of goods will be made here. He raised specific tariffs on specific things for the purpose of promoting manufacture. It is true that at that time the tariff was a much cruder instrument than it is today and that it was imposed mainly for revenue purposes, but the tariffs were raised higher on certain categories of goods because it was considered that with a higher tariff goods would be made in Canada.
It was a good thing, though.

The hon. member is entitled to his own opinion about that. I do not think it would be relevant to debate the question, interesting though it might be. What we are discussing now is whether we ought tc give the Minister of National Revenue the power to raise tariffs on certain imports which now come into Canada because he believes that adequate facilities exist in Canada for the manufacture of those goods. I wish the minister would tell us right now what the things are that the government knows about that it believes there are adequate facilities for so that we will be equipped with knowledge of the facts and will not be simply speculating on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the capacity of Canadian industry is not so limited that in a moment or two I could foresee and prophecy all the developments that will occur in Canadian industry in the years to come. If

one looks today at our achievements compared with those of 20 years ago-
Before C. D. Howe, you mean.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Do not bring C. D. Howe into this. We give him full credit for all that he did. There has been much reference made this afternoon to one debate which is a subject of great embarrassment to my hon. friends opposite so I fail to see why they are bringing in that gentleman's name at the moment.
I should not have liked to make a prophecy 20 years ago concerning developments which have already taken place in Canadian industry. No one can tell what scientific and industry. No one can tell what scientific and technological developments may occur within the next few years. I have already mentioned atomic reactors and thermal generators. These are two things-particularly thermal generators-concerning which it is assumed that within the next few years interesting things will occur because of the development of our economic hydro resources. There may very well be more thermal generators in Canada in the future. If a Canadian firm succeeds in getting a tender on the construction of a thermal generator it can involve thousands upon thousands of man hours of employment. It can succeed in developing an industry here from which at the moment due to competition from outside this country our producers have been excluded from entirely. There has been one made in Canada during the last year. A ruling was made. I made the ruling that it was of a class or kind made in Canada. I am very happy that I did it, too. There was no appeal. There were none of the dire consequences about which we have heard lamentations, griefs, prophecies and fears. All that ensued from it was the provision of employment for Canadians, thousands of Canadian man hours.
That is what this government is going to do. My hon. friends opposite talk about exports and putting on increased costs in relation to the export industry, thereby depriving us of employment. This government is watching that factor. We are not trying to increase the cost of exports. After all, as was said last night, during the relatively short time I have been in office, a period of between three and a half to four years, there have been scores of rulings of class or kind made in Canada. What happened? Under the aegis of my friend the former minister of trade and commerce and now under the new Minister of Trade and Commerce Canada's exports last year were greater than ever before. They were greater than they were under hon. gentlemen opposite who have been weeping saline tears about the future of Canadian
Customs Tariff
exports. My hon. friends do not need to worry about that. We are looking after that matter just as we will look after the question of Canadian employment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The government is not doing very well with respect to employment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
We are doing very well. We have had the two schools of thought among hon. gentlemen opposite, one represented by the hon. member for Essex East, pompous Paul, tramping up and down and ringing the rafters with his howling about unemployment, and the other represented by the member for Bonavista-Twillingate shrieking cries to high heaven about what we are going to do to the Canadian consumers. Hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to make the best of two worlds simultaneously, but they have made an awful mess of both of them.
I certainly do not pretend for one moment that the problem of unemployment is going to be solved by this government unassisted. It requires the co-operation of everybody. We are convinced, however-and we are advised to this effect by labour unions, management and employees-that by means of measures such as this the government is taking steps which will result in increasing the efficiency of Canadian production and in creating additional Canadian employment. Whether that is right or wrong is another matter. Every government has to make decisions on the basis of the best information it can get and on the basis of the technological situation confronting it at the moment. We are convinced that the measure before the committee at the moment is in the best interest of Canadian producers, Canadian employees and Canadians generally, and that instead of interfering with our exports, or prejudicing them, it will add generally to employment and the productive capacity of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, while I admire some of the poetic eloquence employed by the minister in portions of his arguments there is one pattern or thread running through his argument that concerns me very greatly, and that is his insistence on the fact that because we-the minister uses the term "we" meaning the government-are convinced that this legislation is good legislation, therefore he does not have to answer any questions of the opposition or explain precisely and in detail the reasons for the resolution for which the government is seeking the approval of the committee. That is where my difference with the minister and his colleague lies. That pattern has run through the whole of the debate on this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been no such thing.

Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would be good enough to explain what he thinks my colleague the Minister of Finance and I have been doing here in the committee for tne past few days if we have not been answering questions.
Making speeches.

The minister has made little attempt to explain the resolution and the Minister of Finance has devoted his time to vicious attacks on the personalities of those persons who have dared to express a point of view different from that which the minister espouses and he has rarely addressed himself to the resolution before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I have attempted to deal with any questions that have been raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is this not a vicious attack on my personality?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Revenue asked me a question and I am attempting to answer it. I will make no comment about the manners of the Minister of Finance. I am content to leave it to those who read Hansard to form their own assessments as to his manners and conduct as a minister of the crown in seeking the approval of the committee for a resolution brought before it by him. If the hon. gentleman chooses to make personal references to me or about me, that is a matter of complete indifference to me. The minister may make all such references he wishes to, and I hope that will relieve his mind.
Earlier this afternoon when he was asked some very relevant questions the Minister of National Revenue devoted his reply to expounding the argument that no hon. member of the opposition knows anything about this difficult subject whatever and that he and the Minister of Finance do. The hon. gentleman is at perfect liberty to advance that sort of argument if he likes. I for one have always found this legislation quite difficult. I have found the subject complex and difficult. I have never asserted special knowledge of it. I suspect that on occasion the minister has his own problems with it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member is right.

Anyone else who ever deals with it recognizes at once that they have problems with it. However, the minister asked me a question and I felt he was entitled to an answer. The point I want to get at is that there has been a constant repetition by both ministers of the argument that because we, the government, think this is good legislation it should go through, which is not an answer to the questions which have been asked.

A moment ago the Minister of National Revenue said that no one can tell what future developments will be. He was addressing himself to the problem of the terminology custom-made to specifications, I do not think anyone will disagree with that statement too much because technological changes are very rapid, but the point I want to make is that that is not the basis on which to introduce legislation under which the minister is taking away from citizens the right of appeal to a tribunal and arrogating that power to himself as he is effectively doing in these provisions. That is particularly true when you bear in mind the fact that the right involved is that of an appeal by a taxpayer, the consequences of a decision on which may be to impose taxation. It is a very serious thing when such arbitrary power is taken by the minister.
In answer to my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the minister said it was an easy decision to make whether or not goods are custom-made to specifications.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: To order, I said; I said, custom-made to order. It is easy to determine whether or not there is an order.

The whole point and argument back of so many of the kinds of machines coming into plants in the manufacturing business have to do with whether the machinery is something that is custom-made to specifications. You can engage in endless arguments on that subject. I do not want to elaborate the problem here but it is possible to engage in endless arguments as to whether a machine is custom-made to specifications.
With due deference to the minister, it is not an easy decision to make. It is one of the sources of continual representation to departmental officials and to others concerned with the administration of the act. To generalize and to brush it aside and say it is an easy decision to make is not good enough. The decision may be easy enough for the minister to make when he is. dealing with certain of the newer plants such as the atomic energy plant, but let him apply his mind to that other problem, namely the ordinary manufacturing plants which are making consumer goods, and see how difficult it is.
There was some confusion arising out of my remarks last night. I am afraid I did not clearly understand the implications of an interjection by the minister. As a matter of fact, I did not hear it clearly. The interjection was made when I was seeking to point out a distinction between those types of machinery which are not custom-made to specifications, but are used in the manufacturing and production field and are not consumer goods in the ordinary sense at all. My reference was

to such machine tools and machinery. When one reads Hansard today one sees that there was confusion on that point. There was an interjection from the hon. member for Carle-ton which I at least thought had to do with off the shelf goods mainly, but that was another point altogether. The minister says he cannot tell what the development will be in the future; therefore, he is not sure. I deduce from that statement of his that that is why he would need this power. Why is he then taking away from the tariff board the right to make this adjudication? The tariff board is being enlarged and, as I said, I am happy to hear that.
In the concluding part of his argument this afternoon the minister referred to a decision he made that something was of a class or kind made in Canada and everybody was happy and that the results of that decision were very successful. I am not making this as a personal reference to the minister who made that decision, but he had the knowledge, and the staff had the knowledge that that decision was subject to appeal to the tariff board. Let me remind him of that fact. Let me remind him of the fact that the importer also had that certain knowledge in his mind.
I am quite happy that the minister made that successful decision, but let us not be under any confusion about what the effect of this legislation is and what its possible implications may be.
I regret this attempt to accuse anyone who is opposing this method of legislating on this difficult subject of being unfriendly to the economic development of this country or trying to create unemployment in the country. It just is not that way at all. This is difficult legislation on a definition that has caused trouble to succeeding governments over a considerable number of years. Surely what is required is legislation that would provide better certainty and better clarity in the economic field and that would meet the situation and not worsen it.
If he likes the minister can accuse me of having a suspicious mind, I must reiterate that I find this proposed legislation on the points we have been arguing about wholly offensive. I think it is the wrong way to deal with the problem. I think it is a way that is only going to add to the trouble. I think it is a way that is going to, depending on the whim of particular administrations at particular times, lead to an increase in the tariffs on a good many items. That may or may not be desirable. The minister will argue and some will argue that it is in certain cases; but there is this other side of the coin that I want to point out. It may be that improper decisions on this definition will increase the cost of production of our goods.	*
Customs Tariff
Last night I tried to point out to the minister the dangers of having firms, as a result of improper rulings, take machinery that was not quite the best and most efficient they could get and install it in their plants instead of having in those manufacturing plants the most efficient machinery we can possibly get. That is the nub of the problem that secondary industry is having today.
A few minutes ago the minister said something about exports. I invite the minister to examine some of the problems relating to exports. I refer to categories of goods comprising our exports. It is rather difficult to generalize about them, but let the minister examine them in relation to secondary industry in this country. If he does I do not think he will make, shall I say, the same glib statements he has just made on the subject of exports. But more particularly I ask him to consider the implications of wrong use being made of this provision on the cost factor of consumer goods being used in Canada. I point out to him that if those goods are not produced economically and cheaply in Canada, then the pressure is to import those manufactured consumer goods and that is where he gets to the nub of the employment situation in the manufacturing industry. He had better have a bit of a look here and examine rather carefully into the matter.
I wish to raise one other matter. Just before lunch I sought to ask the minister a question when he was dealing with this point. I sought to ask the Minister of Finance a question on the same subject when he was speaking. I refer to the matter of secret information that the Minister of National Revenue has that is not available to the tariff board. The minister pointed out the fact, which is very true as I well know, that the tariff board very frequently gets information from the Minister of National Revenue about quantity of imports, and so on, on which to found their judgment.
I would also like to have this matter clarified. The clear inference from the remarks of both of the ministers was that the tariff board did not also have procedures for getting such confidential information on those matters from his department and, in many cases, confidential information which the Minister of National Revenue does not have in his department. That is the impression which both ministers left, and I do respectfully want to differ from them on this matter of tariff board procedure. I ask them to address themselves to this point and explain to us just what type of confidential information is it that the tariff board has not been able to get that enables the minister to come here now and say he should have the right to make a decision and there should be no

Customs Tariff
appeal to the tariff board. Perhaps I might conclude my remarks for now until I get an answer on that specific point because I should like to have it cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: As I have said and as the hon. member says, it is customary for the tariff board to get confidential information from the Department of National Revenue. It may be that the tariff board has some machinery for the obtaining of confidential information on their own behalf. I have been told, though I do not know this, that the tariff board, although it makes inquiries from our department with respect to information for background purposes, is very reluctant to get information of a confidential nature on its own initiative because it cannot use it publicly. It does not want to be in the position of basing a judgment on confidential information. I have been accused today that I would be doing this, that and the other thing without the right of appeal, but obviously the tariff board does not want to base judgments on confidential information and ascribe its reasons for judgment to confidential information. My understanding of the practice is that the board substantially gets its information from witnesses, and from the Department of National Revenue and they do have-I am not positive about this but I will accept the hon. gentleman's word for it- some machinery whereby the board itself can acquire certain information on a confidential basis.
The point I was getting at was that any confidential information the minister had would presumably have to do with the quantity of imports.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: And also, of course, as to Canadian consumption. Take the question of the 10 per cent. What do you have to do? You have to find out how much is imported and we have the figures. Then you have to get confidentially from various firms, or perhaps not confidentially, the amount that they have manufactured this year and the amount they have sold. We add the two together and that gives you Canadian consumption, and then you ascertain your 10 per cent or more.
That is precisely my point. In determining Canadian consumption one factor is the import data which the Minister of National Revenue has.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Definitely.

It is very definitely a factor and it is information which the minister can easily make available to the tariff board. I have always been under the impression that it was being made available to the tariff board and I have always thought that the

board has very excellent machinery for handling questions of a confidential nature so that there would be no prejudice to the individual firms concerned. I have always thought that the board was an example of a very competent board in that respect and I have a high opinion of their work. However, there is a lot of other information that comes from other sources which has to be gathered together, and from the minister's argument I could not see that he was in any better position to assemble that information than was the tariff board.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Except that I suggest this without interrupting the hon. member, although I suppose I am interrupting him, that the tariff board can get specific information with respect to a specific matter which is before it at a particular time. If they have these powers I am sure they are limited to obtaining information on the specific question. We, on the other hand, and I refer to the officials of the department, because of the fact that we are dealing with all imports at all times and Canadian production generally have this information and are in a position to get information of a confidential nature on a general basis which would not apply to a specific question relating to a specific firm before the tariff board at this particular minute.

I do not want to digress too far into the argument about the tariff board. The board has quite good research facilities and its membership is being enlarged. With deference to the minister, I think I can leave the matter this way, that I find there is some difference in our views as to the possibility of the tariff board doing this job. I think that is perhaps a fair way to leave that point.
There is one other thing. I cannot for the life of me understand this. The Minister of National Revenue spoke several times about the relatively few appeals from departmental rulings. If there are relatively few appeals and the tariff board is being enlarged so it can sit in several panels, what is the logic in taking this appeal work away from the board? Would he explain that? To me it is a simple proposition and I just cannot follow the minister's argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has been
repeated time and again.

I beg to differ. The Minister of Finance would not address himself specifically to that simple proposition. He went into large areas around it with considerable force and vigour but he did not stick to that point and explain it to us in a way that was relevant. I wish he would do so.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Of course, the converse or the other side of the coin is certainly true. If there have been very few appeals exercised, if there has been very little done under the appeal section, then there was no basis for all the blatant outcries we have heard today about the public of Canada being deprived and robbed of something of substance. If my statement is correct and the hon. member accepts it-I am speaking in general terms and not of a specific fraction of one per cent-if there have been very few appeals entered then there has not been this great damage done. We are entering a new field here where undoubtedly there are areas of dispute but we do not want to provide an opportunity for fictitious or fractious appeals in order to delay matters. As my last word before five o'clock and I hope in this debate, although I am perhaps sanguine, I say that these matters on which we are accused of depriving the public of a right of appeal are purely routine statistical matters.
They are not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: You deny that. I am saying that is so. We can spend from now until Christmas arguing about what is statistical and what is not. I am saying that (a) no appeals of any substance have been submitted and (b) if there were appeals they were on statistical matters on which the information is not a matter of argument but a matter of fact, and the Minister of National Revenue is in a better position to produce that evidence than anyone else in the public service.

On the question of appeal, the right of appeal undoubtedly has, as it always has had, a salutary effect on the administrative arm of government. There is no doubt about that. Surely the minister has been a minister of the crown long enough to have noticed that and to have appreciated it. I think the taking away of this right of appeal is going to lead to a dangerous situation and result in damage to our economy. I have further remarks to make, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-12, to provide for pay for statutory holidays for employees and for pay for work performed on statutory holidays.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I again have the honour of introducing the bill before the house. I wish that the government in its wisdom had introduced a bill of its own and that I therefore would not be under the obligation myself of discharging this responsibility. As has been indicated many times previously in this house, the purpose of this bill is to provide that all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction shall receive their regular pay for at least eight statutory holidays each year, without having to work on those holidays. It also provides that when any such employee is required to work on any statutory holiday, as defined in the bill, he shall receive pay for such work at double time in addition to his regular pay for such holiday.
Nothing in this bill affects any provision for statutory holidays with pay enjoyed by any employees where such provisions are more favourable than those enjoyed herein. However, this bill supersedes any provisions which are less favourable than those that are contained in the bill.
After the adoption of this bill on second reading I hope to move that the bill be referred for detailed examination to the industrial relations committee of this house. I know that the bill is a lengthy one and is rather complicated. I feel that a useful service would thus be performed and that the bill ought not to become law until the industrial relations committee has examined it in all the details and implications and has amended it as the committee may desire to amend it. It will then be returned to the house and I hope eventually become law. If, however, the government indicates that it would like to introduce a bill of its own having the same aim, I should be only too happy at any moment's notice to ask leave of the house to have the bill taken off the order paper in order to make it possible for the government to bring in its own bill and we would then be able to deal with the government's proposal.

Private Bills
It is estimated that some 10 per cent ol all employees in Canada do not come under the jurisdiction of any of the provinces but rather come under the jurisdiction of the federal government as far as labour legislation is concerned. Our proposal is one that will guarantee to each and every one of this large group of Canadian workers exceeding several hundred thousand in number the right to a minimum of eight statutory holidays a year; and if for some reason or other they were obliged to work on such holidays they would be entitled to what already prevails in the case of many agreements between employers and employees; that is to say, they would have the right to claim pay for that day as well as double pay for having worked on that particular day. That is in addition to the normal pay for the day would be received by all those who were working.
I know the argument that has been used year after year in opposition to legislation of this kind, namely that matters of this kind are best left to the process of negotiation. However once the people of Canada as a whole accept a certain attitude and once most of the workers involved already have these concessions by the process of negotiation, I submit that it then becomes time for parliament to legislate in order to force, if necessary, those employers who do not comply with accepted standard practice also to grant to their own employees the concessions, rights and privileges that most other workers now have.
Most of our provincial legislatures have now enacted statutory holidays legislation. In the interests of the many workers involved we feel that the national government ought to do the same for workers coming under its particular jurisdiction.
A number of years ago we used to argue for a bill calling for annual vacations with pay for all those workers coming under national labour jurisdiction. At that time the government argued that this matter was best left to the process of negotiation. At this time I want to give the government full marks for having enacted in its first parliament after the 1957 election-I believe it was its first parliament-in fact a vacations with pay bill. I hope the day is not far distant when the government will also see its way clear to round out, if you wish to call it that, its existing labour legislation by providing under law the right of every worker coming within its field of authority to a minimum of eight statutory holidays a year.
I have looked at the debates, especially the one that took place in this house on December 13, 1957 when Mr. Stanley Knowles, the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, introduced a bill almost identical to this

one, as he had so often done in the past. After Mr. Knowles had spoken I am pleased to note that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Small), who is still a member of the house, rose in his place and endorsed the principle of the bill. His main complaint seemed to be that the bill did not go far enough. In his opinion there ought to be legislation to provide for at least one statutory holiday in each and every calendar month. He expressed a little bit of concern about the employer of only one, two or three men or in other words the small enterpriser in Canada. If one looks at the class of workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction he immediately realizes that there are in effect no employers of only a very limited number of men whose employees come under the jurisdiction of the national government.
The bill itself lists most of the major employers of labour who would be affected by labour legislation passed by this parliament. In the main the industries concerned are Canadian railways; Canadian steamship lines; those operating aerodromes, aircraft and lines of air transportation; radio broadcasting stations; banks and banking and enterprises of this kind. It is therefore really not right to argue that this bill would penalize the small enterpriser in Canada inasmuch as the small enterpriser is not involved to' any degree worth mentioning at all. His employees are almost exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
I was also pleased to note that in that debate the spokesman for the Liberal party- I assume he was the spokesman for the Liberal party; I refer to the then hon. member for Kootenay East, Mr. Byrne-also endorsed the principle of the bill and indicated that he had supported the principle of legislation of this kind over a period of many years.
When you have such unanimity in the-house from the spokesmen of all three political parties concerned I feel the government ought not to delay any longer and ought to permit this bill to go through as such, or ought to indicate that it is prepared at a very early date to bring forward legislation of its own having the same ultimate aim in view.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay a vote on this matter, and I also know there are other members who would like to participate in this debate. Therefore I will now close my remarks.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) in introducing this bill. I was struck by one phrase that he used in recommending this bill to the house. He said that most industries have statutory

holidays with pay. He said the idea of this bill-and now I think I am quoting him- is to force those employers who do not conform to accepted standard practices to do so.
I checked with the Department of Labour regarding statutory holidays with pay in connection with non-operating unions and the running trades to try and obtain some facts as to what is now being done and as to what is the custom now. I am told that non-operating unions do have, through collective bargaining, statutory holidays with pay. These unions work on a shift basis. They have regular work weeks and it can be arranged so that men can be off on holidays; and if they are not off, they are entitled to extra pay for those days worked.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. Is the hon. member aware of the fact that the extra gangs employed in such large numbers by the railway companies have no statutory holidays with pay?

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have worked on extra gangs, but this was quite a few years ago. I can say that at that time we had no statutory holidays with pay. Frankly, in my gang we would have thrown the foreman in the river if he had tried to stop us working and had tried to make us just sit around in the bush for a full day. I do not think the point the hon. member has raised is really germane to this bill. Extra gangs are certainly entitled to holidays. Extra gangs are entitled to vacation with pay on the basis of the number of months worked, on a calculated basis, where if they do not get the vacation they receive pay in lieu.
It might well be that something along that line might be worked out at the termination of the job, because the people on extra gangs are not permanent employees of the railroad; that is, they are simply there for one contract, usually that one job only. They are construction workers, and it might well be that something along that line might well be written into this bill. It is not in there now. This bill really deals with permanent employees, employees who have what we might call a year-round job.
When the hon. member talked about forcing employers who do not conform to accepted standard practices, I think he was making a rather drastic statement, because when you look at the list of industries and vocations which do not have statutory holidays with pay you find that they practically all come under the general heading of essential public service.
Private Bills
I suppose that when a man enters the profession of medicine he knows he is going to be called out seven days a week. Shall he charge for a house call on a Sunday three times the charge that he would make for a house call on a Wednesday? The same reasoning can be applied here.
The running trades are paid, not on an hourly basis, not on a daily basis but, as the hon. member knows, on a mileage basis. It is not unusual in a run for a man to accumulate three days' pay in one day. He may be on a mileage basis of 100 miles, and if he travels 300 miles he receives three days' pay. There are lay-offs in the running trades. If people want a holiday, they lay-off; if people are sick, they lay-off. These jobs are based, not on hours but on a mileage standard.
If a train leaves Toronto on Friday and there is a statutory holiday on the Saturday, should it stop or should it carry on? If your telephone goes out of commission, if the power fails in your house and it happens to be a statutory holiday should maintenance crews be available to make the necessary repairs? The hon. member will agree that this must be so. Yet he says that this bill is to force those employers who do not conform to accepted standard practices.
He is trying to apply working conditions, working rights and working methods which you will find in a factory to an essential industry which is based on a 24-hour operation every day, seven days a week.
I suggest that these industries to which I am referring, and which are mentioned in clause 3 of the bill, would like to arrange things so that they did not have to work on holidays, because there must be continuous pressure on them to pay extra for work done on those days, and there must be even more pressure on them from employees who do not want to work on Christmas day no matter how much they are paid. Therefore they must have difficulty in staffing these essential services on family holidays such as Christmas day. So it is not a question of forcing these employers; it is a question that the very facts of life demand that men and women in these essential services have to work on these days.
Therefore we come to the real question. That is, whether employees who have to work on these days shall receive extra compensation for so doing. Let us get to that essential point, not the point that we shall force employers who do not conform to accepted standard practices, but should we legislate that men and women who have to work on holidays shall receive extra pay for working on those holidays?
This is not a question of holidays; this is a question of remuneration, of pay. Questions of pay are properly settled around the

Private Bills
bargaining table through collective bargaining. I think the hon. member has missed that point when he refers to speeches made by other members in this house who have said this is a matter of negotiating between employer and employee. He has thought about it in terms of legislation to give time off on national holidays, rather than legislation which will give extra pay. No matter what we do with this legislation, whether we pass it or not, the same people will be working the day after this legislation is passed as were working the day before. I think that is the criterion. This will not reduce employment on those days, because this employment is in regard to essential services.
So I want to say that viewed in that light I think men and women who work on Christmas day and have to forgo the holiday are entitled to extra compensation, because the following Monday is not as good. Everybody else is back at work. They cannot go on family picnics and family gatherings or to holiday resorts for special events put on that day. They are deprived of the facilities which are made available as special holiday facilities. It must always be borne in mind, of course, that when they entered their avocations they did so in accordance with the conditions of employment existing in those occupations, but since then wages have increased as a result of collective bargaining and fringe benefits have changed, also as a result of collective bargaining, and it may be that collective bargaining could win extra compensation for holiday workers. I think that is the key to the bill and that it should be debated, discussed and decided with that view in mind.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
In rising to speak on this bill I am reminded of the long and often serious struggle working people have engaged in to improve their position in Canada. This is a story which has a peculiar appeal to all of us who know something of the conditions which used to prevail. I have most vivid recollections of those days as told by my father who worked in a stove factory at Guelph when he first came to Canada near the turn of the century. This Conservative party, the party which now forms the government, has a worth-while record with regard to improving conditions and the return for labour in Canada.
The granting of holidays with pay is, for the average Canadian workman, an important part of his daily life. Many of our provinces have recognized that fact in legislation. The legislation varies from one province to another and it is because of this that I think the present bill should receive careful and considerate attention by this parliament. There is a definite need for more universal
recognition of most of what has been included in the bill. However, there is one aspect of this measure which, as it is drawn, raises a question of efficiency of administration, and that is contained in clauses 10 and 11 which to my way of thinking, would make for very wasteful and unnecessary accounting by employers. So that there may be no doubt as to my meaning I think it might be well to read the clauses in full and I make no apology for doing so because I think this measure should be read by everyone who reads Hansard. Clause 10 reads as follows:
(1)	Every employer employing any employee to whom this act applies shall at all times keep a record to be called a "holiday book" showing in the case of each of his employees:
(a)	the name and address of the employees:
(b)	the regular rate of wages of the employee;
(c)	the date of the commencement and termination of the employment of the employee;
(d)	the date of the statutory holiday of the employee in accordance with the act;
(e)	the sum of money paid to the employee in respect of each statutory holiday excluding the sum referred to in clause (f);
(f)	the sum of money paid to the employee in respect of time the employee was required or permitted to work or to be at the disposal of the employer on each statutory holiday;
(g)	the exact hours the employee was required to work or to be at the disposal of the employer on each statutory holiday;
(h)	such other particulars as are prescribed.
(2)	The holiday book may be incorporated in any holiday book or wages book which the employer is required to keep under any other act of parliament.
Clause 11 reads as follows:
The minister or his duly authorized representative may at any reasonable time:
(a)	inspect the holiday book in use by any employer for the time being or any such book used by that employer during the preceding three years;
(b)	require any employer to verify the entries in his holiday book by statutory declaration or in such manner as the Minister or his duly authorized representative may require;
(c)	require any person to furnish, in a form acceptable to the Minister or his duly authorized representative, such information as the Minister or his duly authorized representative deems necessary to ascertain whether the provisions of this act and the regulations are being or have been complied with.
I cannot help but feel that clauses 10 and 11 requiring a separate holiday book are just so much socialist nonsense. I would be happy to see parliament recognize statutory holidays with pay but those two clauses would serve only to set this object apart as something not ordinarily required of a good employer. There is more than enough paperwork undertaken unnecessarily at the present time in the ordinary course of business without adding to that waste by this duplication of an employer's records.
There is another aspect of this situation which may also be worthy of consideration.

These clauses might appear to be just another irritation to a large number of employers in this country who today are overburdened with reports and records many of which are destined never to be consulted. Going through some offices I have been astonished at the weight of dead filing material carried. All this adds to the cost of production, and in this respect the government should be the first to set a good example.
Some time ago I was reading the debates of a few years ago and I noted there has been general agreement on the principle of this bill. Certain days have been set aside for due observance over a long period of time and they have come to mean much to many people of this country. There should be some action taken at federal level to ensure that all our citizens are made aware of these days and their significance in our national life. Legislation such as is contemplated in this field could go a long way toward reaching that objective.
While this bill is necessarily of primary concern to people in the trades and professions I would suggest that one of the statutory holidays which could be considered and observed would be a national farmers' day. The people of Canada have much to be thankful for as far as the contribution of the Canadian farmers to the national welfare is concerned. In many parts of the country there would not be many jobs if it were not for the demand for Canadian goods and services which originates on Canadian farms and in the primary industries. The fact that Canadian farmers have not been as well organized as certain other groups in Canada has contributed to the situation in which the agriculture industry finds itself today, lagging behind the economy of this country. That is one reason for the present difficulties we find in certain industrial areas of our country at the present time.
It is therefore very important, in my opinion, that this parliament take any action that can be taken to bring to the attention of all our people the dependence which all of them have on our primary industries such as agriculture. I should therefore like to move an amendment to this bill. I know this is not the time at which one can move such an amendment but if the proper time were to come the amendment that I should like to move would be that included in the statutory holidays would be a national farmers day. I sincerely elicit the support of all hon. members of this committee for this amendment when it is presented and I hope they will also support the principle of the measure before us.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that the rules do not allow my moving that amendment at
Private Bills
this time. In order that proper consideration may be given this matter I want to say, however, that I am not alone in believing that a holiday known as national farmers' day should be included among our statutory holidays. I have had many hon. members from all parts of Canada and particularly the agricultural areas indicate that they would like to second that amendment.
