speechtext: Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I should like to say that I approve the principle of this bill with the reservations I have set forth today. I also hope that hon. members of the committee will remember the traditions of this party which has placed on the statute books of this country more beneficial labour legislation than was placed on the statute books by any other party in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am also in favour of the principle of this bill but because we have so many unemployed in Canada, instead of paying people triple the wages they earn on a holiday I would rather we give them two extra holidays some other time to help create employment. I do not think we need to offer more inducement to get people to work because they would like to earn three days' wages in one day. I think we should probably have more holidays as a solution for the unemployment problem. I believe that labour and management should co-operate to bring this about.
If each Canadian worker had an extra holiday each month we would create employment for an additional 5 per cent of the working force employing them all year round. This would be a good thing if it could be brought about without increasing the cost of living and without pricing our goods out of the markets of the world. I believe it would go a long way toward solving the unemployment problem in Canada.
Dr. R. Warren James in a brief submitted to the special committee of the other place on manpower and employment on January 25, 1961 pointed out that on September 22, 1960 there were 339,300 unemployed registrants. Of those, 22,500 were workers for whom part time or temporary work was most suitable. Another group numbered 26,800, excluding married women for whom it was not a necessity to work to support themselves or their families. The number of married women for

Private Bills
whom it was not a necessity to work to support themselves or their families totalled 44,500. Those who had worked the full previous week numbered 22,500. A group described as "other registrants" numbered 223,000.
I submit that by having 12 more holidays each year we could employ almost 300,000 more people. Management and labour could share the cost of this 5 per cent increase in the working force. I believe that an increase of 5 per cent in the working force would mean employment for 283,000 additional people.
The solution of the problems of unemployment does not in my opinion rest solely on the government. The labour unions and the working people have a responsibility in this respect. I think if they were really given a chance to agree to such a scheme through their labour unions they would unanimously accept this as a solution.
If we had 5 per cent more people employed in Canada general economic conditions would improve even though it would perhaps mean that those who are working would have to accept a 3 per cent reduction in their wages and that perhaps management would have to absorb 2 per cent of the cost. I think that would assist in bringing about a condition of parity in Canada and the curse of unemployment could become a blessing in that this solution would result in people having more leisure and more time to pursue hobbies and studies, and everyone would have employment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Order. I have been expecting the hon. member to relate the problem of unemployment to this bill. He has failed to do so and I cannot find any connection myself. If I am correct in my understanding this bill does not establish holidays but is for the purpose of seeing that employees under federal labour law receive pay for certain holidays so that the hon. member should really address his remarks to the question of whether or not payment should be made for the holidays already established rather than to the principle of establishing more holidays in an effort to solve the unemployment problem.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was attempting to relate my address to the question as to how to better compensate the people who would work on holidays. Instead of paying them with dollars they would be paid with more leisure time. By giving triple pay we are only creating for those with jobs an incentive to work on holidays at a time when we have so many people out of work.
Double pay is provided for all provincial holidays. This bill really provides for triple

pay. I think this is an exaggerated request. This will help price our goods out of the markets of the world. Today we should attempt to bring down our living costs. We should spread the benefits of labour among all Canadians and not, as it were, create a special monopoly for those who already have jobs. I think it is the duty of those who have jobs to try to spread the benefit to those who are out of work. That is the point I want to make.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF STATUTORY HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is one that has been introduced on many occasions. I well recall my first session in this house. At that time a bill similar to this was introduced by Mr. Knowles, the then member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is now the vice president of the Canadian Labour Congress. I am just wondering how pressing the problem is at this time. I feel that all federal government employees are being justly treated in this matter.
Before I go into that phase of my remarks may I say I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasser-den) who intimated that at one time his father worked for a stove company in Guelph in my riding. I am happy to tell him that the firm is still operating. They have the very best labour relations and they are producing some of the finest stoves in the country.
This problem of federal employees getting paid on statutory holidays is important, but what we must not overlook is that many of these employees of the federal government are doing essential work. The people who are working on statutory holidays are working on very busy days. Their services are needed very badly. I think of the railways and the air lines, the steamship services and such services. They need this help very much on those days, and it is more convenient for them to be given a day off later on which they are given now, as I understand it.
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Regnier) had a good point. He mentioned the fact that it is a case of supplying four days work rather than just more pay at the present time for one individual.
If this bill were to pass it would mean that a person would secure three days pay for one day's work. I think we would have to give serious consideration to this. I agree with the principle of the bill but I feel that certain parts of it should be studied very carefully. No doubt if this bill receives second reading it will go before the industrial relations committee.
Another fact that could come into the picture is this. If one is to be paid three days pay for one day's work, the mercenary angle may become more important than the holiday

angle, and the value of the statutory holidays may become secondary and the mercenary angle foremost.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank the house for having given unanimous consent this morning to revert to motions now in order that I might make a statement.
I wish to inform the house that after careful consideration I have approved the making of an amalgamation agreement between the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the Imperial Bank of Canada for submission to their shareholders as provided by sections 100, 101 and 102 of the Bank Act. The proposed name of the amalgamated bank is the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. In giving approval to the making of this agreement, I have satisfied myself that the public interest will be served in this amalgamation and the interests of the staffs of both banks fully protected.
The banking community is one of the most highly competitive segments of Canadian business. Not only is there internal competition among banks, but they face competition from other lending institutions. Both the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the Imperial Bank of Canada are in a strong financial condition. However, the proposed amalgamated bank, with branches in all Canadian provinces and in several other countries, will be in an even stronger position to provide better and more competitive service to its customers. The amalgamation will enable a broader use of larger domestic resources and provide a more comprehensive international service through association with the extensive branch system of Barclays group of banks.
I am, therefore, of the opinion that the amalgamation would be in the interests of the Canadian public. I am informed that there will be no reduction in staffs or services because of the amalgamation, and indeed it is planned that the new bank will expand its operations on a national basis quite substantially over the coming years.

Mr. Speaker, there is not very much I would care to say on the statement which the minister has made. It is one of importance. I believe

it is some time since we have had an amalgamation of banks such as this in our country.
I am pleased to hear the minister say that this will be in the public interest and that he has satisfied himself that such is the case.
I did note, however, he stated also that it is subject to one of the sections of the Bank Act. As he made his statement I was wondering whether or not legislation will be required to approve the amalgamation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, no legislation is required. The legislation already exists in the three sections of the Bank Act to which I have referred, and this amalgamation is carried out in pursuance of those provisions, and my approval has been given in pursuance of the provisions of these three sections of the Bank Act. They are the same sections that were followed at the time of the amalgamation of the Toronto Bank and the Dominion Bank and the later amalgamation of the Imperial Bank of Canada and Barclays Bank.

Under the provisions of the Bank Act I take it that all that is required is the approval of the minister. Speaking for those of us who sit on this side of the house and without having considered the matter,
I trust, as the minister has said, that this amalgamation will be in the interest of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AMALGAMATION OF CANADIAN BANK OF COMMERCE AND IMPERIAL BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were in a state of excitement behind the curtain for some 15 minutes prior to the minister entering the house, thinking there was going to be some earth-shattering announcement about interest rates, a bond issue or Bank of Canada policy; but we were rather let down in that respect because the minister merely led us in that direction.
However, I must say on behalf of this group that this is a normal development in our present financial and industrial society. We hope that every effort is being made to make certain that the public interest is protected and will be well served; that the clients are protected and will continue to be as well served and that the staffs of this organization will not suffer in any way in respect of salaries, pensions, seniority or things of that sort. That is all I have to say at this time.
